paras: The whipping of Jim Caskey was an attack on a Black man by a band of forty masked men near Douglass Church in Newberry County, South Carolina, on or about July 31, 1885. The men gave Caskey 200 lashes, ordered him to leave the county within twenty-four hours, and also went looking for a second Black man, Lee Clinton, who was not at home. The dispatch explained the attack by saying the two men had talked disrespectfully of white women, and it ran in New York dailies and in Southern weekly news columns.

According to the Newberry dispatch, Caskey and Clinton had been "talking disrespectfully" of "some white women in the neighborhood"; the report gave no source for the charge and named no complainant. A South Carolina state-news column instead said Caskey had been "speaking disrespectfully of ladies in Lancaster."

A party of forty masked men took Caskey from his home near Douglass Church and gave him 200 lashes on his bare back. After the whipping they ordered him to leave the county within twenty-four hours. The same party then went to Lee Clinton's house, but Clinton was absent. The Sun's version of the dispatch, dated July 31, placed the whipping on that day.
No report of arrests, an investigation, or of whether Caskey left the county appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named any of the masked men.

The New-York Tribune printed the Newberry dispatch as a special under the headline "Two Hundred Lashes on His Bare Back," and the Sun ran it the same day as "He Got 200 Lashes." Both versions closed by stating the band's reason as plain fact, the Tribune in the words "These two negroes have been talking disrespectfully of some white women," with no comment on the whipping itself.

In South Carolina, the Fairfield News and Herald of Winnsboro carried the story as a single line in its "News of the State" column, between items on crops, fires and railroads. A condensed version of the dispatch then circulated in a syndicated "Southern News Gleanings" column, appearing in Romney, West Virginia, on August 7, in Rugby, Tennessee, on August 8, and in Maryville, Tennessee, on August 13. No Black-press coverage of the whipping was found.

The Newberry-datelined dispatch located Caskey's home and the alleged remarks in Newberry County, while the Fairfield News and Herald said he had spoken of "ladies in Lancaster"; that item breaks off after "taken from his house" and does not say where the house was. The same South Carolina column separately reported that a Lee Clinton, "colored," and Tom McCardell had a "shooting match" in Lancaster over indecent remarks about one man's wife, a case that "was compromised"; the coverage does not show whether this was the Clinton the band sought.

framing.detail: The New York papers ran the dispatch under headlines on the lashes and repeated without comment the band's reason that 'these two negroes' had talked disrespectfully of white women.

Tennessee and West Virginia weeklies reprinted the dispatch in a 'Southern News Gleanings' column.
